data.title: How ScratchNews was Made
data.summary: This article is about how ScratchNews appeared as an idea, then became a website, and turned into what it is now today.
data.content:
Hello!

In the last few days, ScratchNews has grown very fast: from 10 daily visitors and 10 users, to over 30 daily visitors and 16 users. The website has just hit it's first 100 visitors!... But how was ScratchNews made? How did it evolve into the platform people know today? How did this all happen?

That's what we're gonna answer today. We're gonna look at how ScratchNews was made, it's growth, and how it turned from a simple idea into a tiny community dedicated to informing the misinformed.

Part 1: The Ban

On March 24th, 2026, my Scratch account "suswhopper123" was permanently banned for the second time. This was after I've done a forum joke, that turned into an alert, that ultimately turned into a permanent block.

I was devastated. At that point, I loved Scratch more than anything else, but this ban changed the history of my entire Scratch account. Some of my greatest life achievements were made on Scratch. Scratch was such a big part of my life that I've never pictured getting it taken away.

As any Scratcher would do, I appealed to the Scratch Team, hoping for a response or something I could do to get unbanned. They requested me to use a parent/guardian email account, and I did exactly that. However, it took weeks to get a response back from them.

This was one of the worst times I could've got my Scratch account back. Final tests were coming up, and I was more stressed than ever, especially in French and History: two of the most boring classes ever. I had to be more prepared than ever, when I didn't have motivation to continue living.

Almost all hope was lost. My screen time skyrocketed. I spent my free time watching videos on Viber's video player when I haven't even made my maths homework *my favorite class is maths*. I've went back to visiting c.ai. My grades were in a free fall, from 9s and 10s, to 7s and 8s, to 6s and 7s...

Yet one day at the end of April, as I scrolled through Youtube via Yandex Browser, one video appeared that would change the trajectory of my life; "Every stage of self-improvement explained". I've realized that I was sitting in stage 1 this entire time. So I started stage 2. I started self-improving.

Part 2: The Self-Improvement Era

I didn't really have a plan to change my life. I just saw that "Better Ideas", the man in the thumbnail, was running in Stage 2. So I did the same. I started running.

At first, it was 5 laps (~1.7 km) a day. This tiny amount that I did every day signaled a message to me: "I'm doing something to improve myself, so I won't quit at least until summer". So I kept going.

I was watching more self-improvement videos, more educational videos and I started testing myself on classes I hated using AI and multiple-choice questions. While none of the questions in the final tests were multiple-choice, the results were astonishing: 9 in history and 10 in French.

This self-improvement era pushed me to do a lot of things. At the start of June, I was now doing 20 laps (~7 km) a day. I was reading financial books. I was starting to become someone else.

I still wasn't well with Scratch though. Scratch Team went from "parent email" to "parent voicemail" to "child email" to "unresponsive". This phase wasn't perfect.

At the end of June, I had an idea for a website called "ScratchNews". The idea was for a Scratch website with news and entertainment on it in the form of articles, mixed with a social side of the platform.

The idea wasn't new; it was simply just a new mix. ScratchViews for the name inspiration, news website for how articles should be formatted and basic features, Facebook for inspiration on social features, and whatever else came into my mind. ScratchNews was still one of those ideas that I thinked about when I was running, it still wasn't executable. But I wanted it to be.

Part 3: Early ScratchNews Development

I was familiar with hosting websites, I had around 3 of my own for free. I switched from x10 hosting to InfinityFree, because I would much rather have a .gamer.gd domain instead of .x10.mx. The best free domain for ScratchNews was .freedev.app, and with no money, no card and no donations, I started writing PHP in an AI File Manager to see my website bloom. I also started branding ScratchNews and using Claude for some bug fixes and features here and there.

The scratchnews.freedev.app domain started in July 5th, 2026. In that same day, articles were added, and I made the first ever article: Welcome To ScratchNews.

I was adding features very quickly to ScratchNews. Just 2 days after the initial website launched, on July 6th, we added accounts. On July 8th, Link Text and fixed admin tab showing to non-admin users. And on July 12th, we got outr first ever user: @xapneb.

ScratchNews didn't even have 5 users, yet it felt like it was thriving. I was constantly making articles for my users and always asking them for feature and article ideas. And then, things sped up.

Part 3: ScratchNews Development and Growth

On July 17th, 2026, ScratchNews had hit its 5th user: @I_LOVE_FLIP_CLOCKS. ScratchNews also got it's first namesniped user, @abc, which I quickly deleted.

I was still constantly advertising the website to Discord servers and friends. On July 24th, ScratchNews hit 10 users. But just a day after that, we hit 14. Some people were making articles, some were engaging with them, and the platform was alive.

And then the numbers. The numbers don't lie. Since July 23rd, we've hit a consistent 30 visits every single day. Yesterday we even hit our peak: 35 new visits!!!

We added many features since then. Images, Explore, an API, we're still doing everything to satisfy our users.

But the user growth is random! One day we have 4 new users in a day, the next we have none. One day we have our peak, the next we're just shy of 30 daily visits. If you'd like to support us, the best way you can is by making a ScratchNews account, as we're still a tiny website. Your feedback, opinions and attention is the most valuable thing I could have; if you have any article ideas, feature ideas, or just want to like and share this article, you can do so right now.


Thanks for reading! Have a good day!

data.title: Itchy: Mobile Scratch done Right
data.summary: This article talks about "Itchy", a popular third-party app that reimagines the Scratch Mobile experience. We'll review it, talk about its benefits and weaknesses, and ultimately see if it's better than Scratch mobile.
data.content:
As a Scratcher, Scratch on a phone can be tough. Pinch just to get the full image of the Scratch project while it's running, flip your phone just to see inside the project... and don't even tell me about surfing the forums, accessing the editor and coding.

One time someone commented on my game, "Primary", that I should add a speedrun record time as a cloud variable. I was in a hotel, and, without a proper PC, I spent over an hour trying to implement the code to my Scratch project. All on my mom's phone. You can imagine the hassle.


However, something can fix this! There is a third-party app called "Itchy", an app that tries to fix this experience using the Scratch API and design, and bring some new features along the way. In this article, we'll review it, view the pros and cons, and if it ultimately is better than Scratch on mobile.

Part 1: Installing the App

You can install the app for free, in the App Store or Play Store. It's 31/54 MB (depends if you're using Android or iPhone) and it's made by David Banziger.

Part 2: Features

This is how the app normally looks like (screenshot taken from FANJOUA, formerly McVincient):

As you can see, the design is liquid-glass like and heavily relies on rounded corners for its UI. The app runs projects in Turbowarp, a popular website that speeds up Scratch projects by orders of magnitude using JavaScript. The app also has a built-in controller and joystick, similar to ScratchGo, a mobile Scratch player, which we actually made an article about.

Another feature that Itchy has is the "Users" section in Search. It searches for users similar to the search query you gave, and it gives a direct link to them.

What's also interesting in Itchy is the profile page of a user. It's slick, minimalistic, and social-media-like: the follower counter is approximated, it says the year joined instead of account age.

Sometimes, Itchy runs multiple tabs so that scrolling between them is easier (for example, in a studio page). But this can be laggy on lower-end devices, so it's best to use it on studios with few projects.

Now for the messages! The messages are infinitely scrollable, meaning that you don't have to click a "load" button to get more of them. You can directly sort messages by category with the Message Category buttons (Studios, Comments etc.)

These are most of the features Itchy offers; now let's see the pros and cons.

Part 3: Itchy Pros and Cons

Pros:

  1. Refreshed Web Scratch Experience
  2. Refined Explore, Search and Profile pages
  3. Joystick and controller for mobile users to play PC games
  4. Sort by "Users" on search

Cons:

  1. No Forums, Editor or My Stuff
  2. UX may be harder to adapt to for some users
  3. Controller/Joystick may not have all game keys
  4. May look too minimalistic for some

Part 4: Is Itchy worth it?

It's only worth it if you're looking for the social stuff of Scratch. You may use it with the website itself combined, but if you do not like the design you may not use it at all. It's a step in the right direction, but the step didn't got us to the finish line.

That's all for this article!

Thanks for reading! If you like reading about opinions and tools, check out "ScratchGo: The Mobile Scratch Player We Actually Needed" or "Scratch Moderation Needs Reform" for moderation. As always, make sure to like, comment and share! Thanks for being a part of ScratchNews!

data.title: Scratch Membership is discontinued: What actually happened, and what it means for the Site
data.summary: This article explains why Scratch Membership was discontinued, what it means for the website, and what past Membership users should expect.
data.content:
Recently, the Scratch Membership got discontinued. But why? Why was it discontinued, what is it, what features did it gave and what will happen? This article answers these questions.

What was the Scratch Membership?

The Scratch Membership was a subscription service that allowed Scratchers to get additional perks, while also being a donation for the Scratch site itself. It was released in early 2025 for $35/year or $150 for a lifetime, before being increased in 2026 to $50/year or $200 for a lifetime.

What were the perks of the Scratch Membership?

The perks of Scratch Membership were:

1: Story Xperiential

Membership members could get access to a Story Xperiential preview for free, including a year of access to it for $25, an 83% discount. However, non-Scratch Membership members could get access to the full program for $113 rather than $150.

2: Exclusive sprites

Scratch Membership members had access to "exclusive sprites": 2 new sprites called Zepto and Milli, and Yooka Laylee sprites from a partnership with Playtonic. The sprites couldn't be seen in the Sprite Library by non-Scratch Membership members, but they could still be backpacked and used anywhere.

3: Scratch Store discounts

Scratch Membership members received 10% off the majority of items in the Scratch Store at any time, and 25% off after the announcement of discontinuation. Members located in the United States also received free shipping with orders of $50 or more.

4: Member-exclusive merch

Scratch Membership members could purchase exclusive Scratch Member-themed merch (like a Scratch dog collar, a Scratch baby crib, or a Scratch hoodie with the image The Creation Of Adam, except the two faces were replaced with the Scratch Cat face)

5: Scratch Membership newsletter

Self-explanatory. Not neccessary anymore, since you know about ScratchNews.

6: Profile/Editor cosmetic changes

Membership members could toggle cat ears that appeared around their profile picture and a membership badge that appeared next to the follow button on their profile. They also had a purple "Member" badge that appeared next to their username and on the forums, which couldn't be disabled.

On the editor, Membership members could enable the cat blocks that appeared in April Fools using a new "Theme" menu in the editor, accessible from the Settings drop-down.

When and how was the Scratch Membership discontinued, and what should past Membership users expect?

On May 20th, 2026, the Scratch Team announced that "we've learned that the current perks-based membership program is not the right fit for the Scratch community" and on the same day, the ability to purchase Membership was removed. The announcement stated that the Membership perks will be soon available for everyone, and that there will be a new program for donors; and once the new program launches, past Lifetime members will have some perks in the new program.

On June 15th, 2026, the Scratch Membership program was discontinued. As promised, the cat blocks, cat ear frames, and Zepto and Milli sprites became available for everyone. The purle member badges and the badge shown next to the follow button on members' profile pages, was removed.

Past Membership users should expect having perks in a new Scratch donation program (when it will be launched).

That's all!

-> Thanks for reading this article! Make sure to like, comment and share!

If you like reading about controversial Scratch topics, you can also check out "Scratch Moderation Needs Reform" (about moderation), "The Mystery of Fake Scratch Geometry Dash" (about fake Scratch Geometry Dash games), or "What happened with Explore?" (about the Explore page). Thanks for reading, and have a good day!

data.title: The Mystery of Fake Scratch Geometry Dash
data.summary: This article is exploring the fake Scratch versions of Geometry Dash, how they get used in fake game websites for ads and money, and why some Geometry Dash projects got taken down.
data.content:
Hello!

If you're a Scratcher, you may have played the most popular games on Scratch a lot, such as Paper Minecraft, Ninja or even less popular games like Bloons Tower Defense Scratch 4, and you've probably also played a very popular Scratch project series: Geometry Dash.

There are many Geometry Dash Scratch projects out there: most are trying to mimic editor or online levels, some go the extra mile and make a level themselves, but either way, the Geometry Dash Scratch community is very active right now. But the most popular creators on it are getting their projects banned; this article will tell you why and how are Geometry Dash projects used.

Who plays Geometry Dash Scratch projects?

This may sound like a dumb question, but the answer to it is more important than you might think.

While Scratchers do play these Geometry Dash copies and remixes, other third parties are using them for profit: game websites.

Take a look at what happens when I search for "Geometry Dash" on Google. Yes, you might see the official Geometry Dash website, the Steam version, and the Wikipedia article at the right... but oh, what's that first result? "Geometry Dash Unblocked"?

What in the CrystalKeeper7 is this monstrosity? This, my friends, is Fake Geometry Dash. While the game itself wasn't made on Scratch, people oftentimes create fake websites and games titled as "Geometry Dash" then do all that it takes to get it at the top of the search results. We weren't lucky to get a Scratch version, though; don't worry, we'll get one in a minute.

There it is! Geometry Dash Scratch! It doesn't take a detective to play those fake copies of Geometry Dash. So what's going on?

As I've said before, people oftentimes create fake Geometry Dash websites. Fake Geometry Dash websites need fake Geometry Dash games, though. And who has the largest database of free, Geometry Dash looking projects that look good enough? Scratch! Imagine, program, share!

So, the people who make these websites go on a journey, and steal Geometry Dash projects from little children like you. Then they grab the fake games with fake images, slap them on their website, do a little ads here, a little popup there, some SEO over there and BAM! - you've got fake Geometry Dash Scratch games on fake Geometry Dash websites.

RobTop, the developer of the official Geometry Dash, does make an effort to remove these fake websites and games. That's why he sometimes does this with...Scratch projects.

How does RobTop delete Scratch Geometry Dash projects?

In the User Content section of Scratch's Terms Of Service, it has been said that "The Scratch Team is not responsible for other users' content, including editing it. The Scratch Team has the right to take down content that they believe violates the Terms Of Service." What did they also say in User Content? "5. You Must Have Rights to the Content You Post; User Content Representations and Warranties" In that section, the user automatically agrees that their content does not cause the Scratch Team to violate any laws or require them to pay any fees." What does this all mean?

Well, this means that your project can be taken down at any time, especially if it violates any laws. Last time I heard, copyright is a law. So that means that if your project violates copyright laws or you're not the copyright holder, then say goodbye to it.


RobTop is the copyright holder of Geometry Dash. This means that, if Scratch Geometry Dash projects are being used for commercial purposes, he can just take them down. If a Geometry Dash website uses a Scratch Geometry Dash project and also hosts ads on it, then the website is using Geometry Dash Scratch projects for commercial purposes. Which means that, RobTop can just request to take down any website or Scratch project that uses Geometry Dash for commercial purposes/with ads. And since a big chunk of these websites use ads to pay the bills.. you see where this is going.

So, RobTop requested the Scratch Team to take down many Geometry Dash Scratch projects to be taken down. This includes the Geometry Dash projects made by famous Scratchers like griffpatch, CrystalKeeper7, iPhone_ATT_TWC15, hoppingicon, and anyone in between. Since the Scratch Team is obligated to take down Scratch projects that violate copyright laws.. they did the only thing they could.


That's all for this article.

Sad. But you wanna know what's also sad? Scratch Moderation! In this article, one of our ScratchNews users tells us what's wrong with the current state of moderation in Scratch, his experience, and what could Scratch Team do.

Make sure to like, comment, and share this article with your fellow Scratchers! Bye!

data.title: ScratchGo: The Mobile Scratch Player We Actually Needed
data.summary: About the website ScratchGo, a site that lets you play almost any Scratch game with smooth, custom mobile controls!
data.content:
So a while back I came across this brand new website called ScratchGo (developed by FireWorks Studios). The website claimed that you could play any Scratch game on your iPhone! So I decided to give it a go. It was amazing! The controls were super smooth and I was able to play Paper Minecraft (by griffpatch) with ease!


The website is very sleek and modern and works on both Android and iOS! It works by pasting the project link and then you can control it with the large arrow keys and the joystick placed under the project sandbox.


There is also an experimental mode that lets you add buttons and edit the sizes of them. You can also modify the buttons to make it so that when it's clicked, it can emulate any button! For example, you can make a large button that when it's pressed, would simulate pressing 'E' on a keyboard!


Sadly, the website doesn't seem to be getting updated anymore as of July 2026, but it has more than enough features to run almost any Scratch project!


Fun fact: ScratchGo is actually built on top of TurboWarp, which is probably why the games run so smoothly! It was made by a solo developer, and it even went viral for a bit after a Scratch YouTuber made a video about it, doubling the site's traffic in just 3 days!


One thing to keep in mind is that ScratchGo works best with keyboard-controlled games, so mouse only projects might not work quite as well. But for anything keyboard based, it is one of the best ways to play on a mobile device!


So go on your mobile device, and try that Scratch project you've always wanted to try on it!

 

Link to the website: https://scratchgo.app/

data.title: Scratch Moderation Needs Reform
data.summary: Many Scratch users believe the platform's moderation system is too strict because projects can be removed instead of allowing creators to fix small issues. One example is KPPKAUNG's ChatGPT project, a fully working Scratch chatbot that gained over 7,000 views and many loves and favorites before being removed. The Scratch Team claimed it contained a link to a commercial website, but the "link" was not an actual URL — it was simply the project name "ChatGPT," which they associated with the real we
data.content:
Scratch Moderation Needs Reform

Scratch is an amazing platform that has helped millions of people learn programming, but many users believe its moderation system has become too strict and unfair.

A common complaint from the community is that projects are sometimes removed instead of allowing creators to fix small issues. Many Scratchers have experienced losing projects, views, and community support because of decisions that could have been solved with a warning.

One example is my own project. I created a fully working ChatGPT project in Scratch that gained over 7,000 views, along with many loves and favorites. It was an impressive project that demonstrated what could be created with Scratch. However, it was removed on June 15, 2026.

The removal message stated:

"The Scratch Team has removed your project because it contains a link to a commercial website. Please note that we do not allow commercial activity on Scratch due to security and privacy concerns..."

However, the "link" mentioned was not an actual website link. I never added any URL such as "hello.com" or any external website. Scratch considered the name "ChatGPT" itself as a link to the real ChatGPT website.

Instead of removing the entire project, a better solution would have been to request a simple name change or whatever they think is being a 'link'. Losing a project with over 7,000 views and many loves and favorites because of a name issue feels unfair, especially when the problem could have been fixed easily.

Scratch needs moderation, but it should focus more on helping creators correct mistakes rather than immediately removing their hard work. A warning-first approach would protect the community while also respecting the time and effort creators put into their projects.
data.author: KPPKAUNG_YT

data.title: The Evolution Of Scratch: Scratch 3.0, Modern Scratch Updates and the "downfall" of Scratch (Part 4)
data.summary: This article is about the launch evolution of Scratch 3.0, also known as Scratch 3. It is Scratch's current version, and had some updates from 2019 until now; this article talks in depth about it.
data.content:
This is Part 4 of an article series, "The Evolution Of Scratch." See other parts:

Before Scratch Released (Part 1)

Scratch website, community, and Scratch 1.0-1.4 (Part 2)

Scratch 2.0, Scratch's "Peak" and Scratch Community (Part 3)


Scratch 3.0, Modern Scratch Updates and the "downfall" of Scratch

Preface

You love it or you hate it, but Scratch 3.0 is still the current update of Scratch. We've already talked about every Scratch update except 3.0, you can check the past articles above for the links. In this article, we'll talk about the new editor and website changes, the drama over the years, the changes, and everything you need to know about Scratch 3.

Part 1: Development of Scratch 3.0

In May 2016, the Scratch Team announced a partnership with Google to create Scratch Blocks, the new design for the up-and-coming Scratch 3.0 blocks. Later in 2016 and 2017, many changes were made to the User Interface.

On January 18th, 2018, a preview version of Scratch 3 was released at preview.scratch.mit.edu. On August 1, a Beta version was released at beta.scratch.mit.edu that added new extensions, and the Scratch 3.0 Beta forum was created for feedback on Scratch 3.0.

During the transition from Scratch 2.0 to Scratch 3.0, Scratch was in a special maintenance mode for a few days. It was then launched at Jaunary 2nd, 2019.

Part 2: Scratch 3.0 Editor and Website

While Scratch 3.0 was a tinier update compared to Scratch 2.0, it was still a major one. The editor had a massive change, and the code panel was now one the left and the runner on the right: just like in Scratch 1.4.

The new blocks added in Scratch 3.0 are the "go to []" and "go [] () layers" blocks, the costume [] and backdrop [] blocks, set/change pitch/pan effect blocks, set drag mode [] block, () contains ()? block, and the delete all of [] and item # of () in [] list blocks. There was also added the online? block, but released much later (January 2026).

Fonts were replaced with the classic 9: Sans Serif, Serif (Times), Handwriting, Marker, Curly, Pixel, Chinese, Japanese and Korean.

The Scratch 3.0 website was redesigned again, adding a banner and changing the design of many pages; but some pages, like the Discussion Forums, Statistics, Profile Pages and My Stuff still had the old design. This was because the update was made in a rush; the old Scratch 2.0 runner was in Flash, and Flash was going to be discontinued in 2020.

Part 3: Scratch 3 Updates: from 2019 to now

On January 9th, 2019, the Scratch Team fixed many bugs Scratchers had reported in the editor and the website. Some of the bugs were projects getting stuck on the loading screen, and the love and favorite buttons not showing up.

In early-mid January 2019, the front page banner was changed from "The new Scratch is here!" to "Create stories, games, and animations" and "Share with others around the world". The front page banner changed to the modern one you see when you're not logged into an account.

On August 1st, 2019, the sound editor was improved, adding the copy/paste/select sound features, and basic keyboard shortcuts to the editor.

On February 13th, 2020, the Paint Editor introduced the Costume Centering update that lets you center costumes more easily.

On May 18th, 2020, the Paint Editor allowed to zoom out beyond the canvas and be seen on different browser sizes.

On July 6th, 2021, the Studio Pages were visually updated to the Scratch 3.0 design and the number of managers that a studio could have was limited to 40. The ability for New Scratchers to create studios was removed, managers could no longer edit the title, description, and thumbnail of studios and a limit of 25 replies to a studio was added.

On June 28th, 2023, the project editor was updated with High Contrast Blocks, and changed the navigation bar from blue to purple.

On November 6th, 2024, the Tutorial Menu was reorganized and an additional confirmation message was added when trying to delete a sprite.

On December 16th, 2024, the Debug button was added and the Community Guidelines and Ideas pages were redesigned.

On October 7th, 2025, the Face Sensing Extension was added.

On January 29th, 2026, the "online?" block was added.

Part 4: Scratch drama and controversy

On May 7, 2022, the creator of the fan-made Scratch modification TurboWarp announced that the Scratch Team was making some changes to Scratch's API, and that the bug which allowed users to view unshared projects using various software (such as TurboWarp, forkphorus, and even Scratch 3.0's development builds) would likely be removed on an unknown date. This sparked a small outcry, as some Scratchers were arguing that because of this update because it could arise some problems (such as removed ability to view harmless unshared projects). Nonetheless, on November 10th, 2022, the ability to view unshared projects via API was removed.

In November 2024, a job listing on the Scratch Foundation website for salesforce administration was discovered by Scratchers that hinted at a Scratch 4.0 "integrating creative AI". This mention of AI led to significant backlash within the Scratch community.

On the 22nd January, 2026, the Terms of Service was updated to explicitly state that Scratch could use content in projects and other parts of the website to train AI models, supposedly claiming this helps them with "exploring new AI-powered tools designed to support this community with even more ways of creating."

Some users have complained that, allegedly, the appeals system is broken and they never get a response to their appeals after months of waiting, although this has been confirmed to have happened a few times. The Scratch Team has also confirmed that as of July 2022, they are often taking several weeks to respond to appeals due to limit resources for handling them.

Part 5: The End of Scratch History

While Scratch 3.0 was a big update, it sparked more backlash than ever before. We have talked about every single known Scratch version possible, from Scratch 0.x to 3.0. If you want to know more about the future versions of Scratch (like 4.0) visit the article "What We Know About Scratch 4.0". And as always, make sure to like, comment, share, and have fun in ScratchNews!
data.author: TODB

data.title: The Evolution of Scratch: Scratch 2.0, Scratch's "Peak" and Scratch Community (Part 3)
data.summary: This article is about the evolution of Scratch 2.0, also known as Scratch 2. Many people consider it the "golden age" of Scratch.
data.content:
This is part 3 of an article series, "The Evolution Of Scratch." See other parts:

Before Scratch Released (Part 1)

Scratch website, community, and Scratch 1.0-1.4 (Part 2)

Scratch 3.0, Modern Scratch Updates and the "downfall" of Scratch (Part 4)


Scratch 2.0, Scratch's "Peak" and Scratch Community

Preface

You heard about the so-called "golden age" of Scratch? High-quality projects everywhere, a shining explore page, a happy community and the supposed "best Scratch version ever"? No? Well, some Scratchers think that Scratch 2.0 was the best ever update to Scratch. Since we're talking about the evolution of Scratch and just made an article about Scratch 1.x, it's time to embrace the most nostalgic era of Scratch: Scratch 2.

Part 1: Development of Scratch 2.0

In late 2009, John Maloney, the lead programmer of Scratch since 2003, started development on a flash version of what will become Scratch 2.0 titled "BlocksEngine". The blocks in BlocksEngine looked almost the same as in the final release of Scratch 2.0, and the engine was very basic: no sprites, only simple shapes could be drawn using preset blocks.

The very first Scratch 2 versions were named "iScratch V2", and developed from May-August 2010. The versions were developed in collaboration with the Playful Invention Company (PICo).

Scratch 2 was announced in January 2010, but users weren't allowed to see it until August 2010. In that time, the experimental viewer went public as a basic engine for what would become Scratch 2. It was nearly as basic as BlocksEngine, and it lacked costume editing, comments, and much more.

In February 2011, the Scratch Flash Player was introduced in the Scratch website. Before, projects shared on the Scratch website were running in the Java player; Flash was a much faster way to run projects and went on to be the player that ran Scratch 2.0 projects.

On February 16th, 2012, Scratch 2 entered alpha development. The public only saw a mention of Scratch 2 way later in Scratch Day 2012. During that time, the alpha version of Scratch 2 (alpha.scratch.mit.edu) was available for a few days.

On December 2012, Scratch 2.0 entered beta development, though public beta testing began on January 28th, 2013. The Scratch Team migrated all the users, projects and comments to the beta website, at beta.scratch.mit.edu, to prepare for this date. The Beta website went down on May 6th, 2013 for Scratch 2.0 to officially launch at May 9th, 2013.

Part 2: The Scratch 2.0 editor

If Scratch 1.4 was big, Scratch 2.0 was massive. It had the most features out of any Scratch version; not even Scratch 3.0 was that big of an update compared to 2! The features that were added IN THE EDITOR are...

...Backdrop Name, Backpack, CLONING (yes it didn't exist before), Cloud Variables/Data, Custom Blocks (now known as "my blocks" or "function blocks"), show/hide lists, SOUND EDITOR, Time Blocks, Username Block, VECTOR + BITMAP EDITOR, VIDEO SENSING and much more!!

Scratch 2.0 gave users capabilities to push the editor to new heights, create 2.5D and 3D projects, have massive performance boosts from the "Run Without Screen Refresh" option in custom blocks, use pen blocks to their full power and create realistic effects with them, use clones to make what were once sprite-heavy projects block-heavy projects, use the time block to detect timezone, etc.

But we're not done yet! We still have to look at the Scratch website, which had new users and projects by the second...

Part 3: The Scratch 2.0 website

While the editor had huge changes, the website had massive changes, too. Below is a showcase of the Scratch 2.0 homepage:

As you can see, the website didn't had massive UI changes since 2.0 to now. There was a 'Welcome To Scratch!' page for new Scratchers that can be replaced with 'What's Happening?' once the user gets the Scratcher rank, featured projects had the familiar UI of today, yet many features were added in the Scratch website that we now take for granted. Some of these features are...

...Customizable User Pages, Following System (followers didn't exist before this), Project Notes And Credits being separated from Instructions, Redesigned Comment Replies (@username shows who you're replying to), Studios (that replaced galleries), @username to link someone to their user page in a comment, and Student and Teacher accounts.

Now that we've talked about the editor and the website, let's talk about the most prominent drama and controversy of that time!

Part 4: Scratch 2.0 Drama and Controversy

We can't talk about Scratch Drama without talking about FNAF ("Five Nights At Freddy's"). FNAF was a 2014 survival point-and-click horror game. It got popular pretty fast, but it soon got the worst reputation out of any horror media due to the intense jumpscares and gory backstory. The Scratch Team search-banned the term (meaning that people cannot search for it without getting empty results), and said in a public forum that they're not gonna ban all FNAF games outright, because it is possible to make a game that follows the Community Guidelines with FNAF. On November 16th, 2015, speakvisually announced that FNAF lead to massive issues such as nightmares and some school districts banning Scratch, which meant that FNAF had to be restricted. From then, projects that serve as simulations or recreations of FNAF games are no longer allowed from the Scratch website.

On July 5th, 2017, the "Discuss" and "Help" links was removed from the Scratch website header, in favor of a new page, "Tips". This, in just a few hours, sparked massive outcry among much of the community and Scratch forum users, with many users using the hashtag "#Bring_It_Back" and even changing their signatures in favor of one side or another.

On November 30th, 2017, the Scratch Team announced that advertising or naming third-party browser extensions (including userscripts) made for Scratch was disallowed due to the concern of some scripts/extensions can collect private data without the users knowing. The Scratch Team has said that using extensions is fine, but naming or advertising them was not. Within 24 hours, this started up many complaints about the new policy.

Part 5: Scratch Growth and Statistics

To show you just how big Scratch 2.0 was, let's look at some statistics in Scratch in that time.

In early 2014, Scratch reached 6 million registered users. Two years later, it hit 10 million users and over 800,000 new projects every month: one project every 3.2 seconds. In 2017, the platform reached 20 million users, and in the February-August period about 3 million users; one new user every 6.05 seconds. In 2018, the platform hit 30 million users, right before Scratch 3.0 launched.

Part 6: The End of the Golden Age

That's all for this article! In the next one, we'll talk about the modern Scratch 3.0 and all of the other stuff with it: the editor changes, the community and the massive shifts (for example, Scratch becoming unaffiliated with the MIT). We'll talk about everything that happened since January 2019 since now! Make sure to hit that like button, *lol* share this on Scratch, comment, reply and have fun! Thanks for reading!!!

data.title: The Evolution of Scratch: Scratch website, community, and Scratch 1.0-1.4 (Part 2)
data.summary: This article series is about the evolution of Scratch, from the early 2000s to the biggest programming language for kids.
data.content:
This is part 2 of an article series, "The Evolution Of Scratch." See other parts here:

Before Scratch released (Part 1)

Scratch 2.0, Scratch's "Peak" and Scratch Community (Part 3)

Scratch 3.0, Modern Scratch Updates and the "downfall" of Scratch (Part 4)


The Scratch website, community, and Scratch 1.0-1.4

Part 1: The launch of the Scratch Beta website, Scratch 1.0 and 1.1

On May 15th, 2007, the first ever stable version of Scratch released to the public: Scratch 1.0.

Scratch 1.0 was the first ever Scratch editor version to be used in the Scratch website, yet it still was in a huge experimental phase. The sound pallete had new blocks that worked with the ScratchMoviePlayerMorph morph. Morphs were like sprites with extra capabilities, features, or pre-made assets: ScratchMoviePlayerMorph was a Scratch morph that allows movies from a computer to be played in Scratch.

The Sensing category had new camera blocks, but they did not work properly. Scratch 1.0 was very similar to Scratch 26Dec06; but what wasn't similar, was the Scratch website.

At this point, the Scratch website was still in beta, but it had a blog. Resources like tutorials, project ideas and group activities were links in the middle-left, while the first Scratch forums were on the top-right. Users could email the Scratch developers, upload their own projects to the website, search projects and download them; but not play them in the browser. The Scratch website wasn't meaningfully updated until Scratch 1.4.

Scratch 1.1 was released in May 2007 and didn't have many improvements, but a new block and UI features. It introduced the first "cap block" (stop script) and the "repeat until" block. Users could now share the projects they made to the Scratch website directly through the editor, add project notes and tags.

Part 2: Scratch 1.2 and 1.3

Scratch 1.2 Beta was released in October 29th, 2007, 1.2 in December 2nd, 2007, and 1.2.1 in June 6th, 2007.

Scratch 1.2 added the "costume #" block, tempo and volume blocks were added, the comment block and the () of () sensing block was added. Scratch 1.2.1 had bug fixes, such as tempo value being a global value instead of local, added the rest for () beats block, etc.

Scratch 1.3 was launched on September 2nd, 2008. It did had significant features, such as the show/hide variable blocks, "C" blocks (blocks that wrap around the blocks beneath them), comments in the modern form, lists and the file selector. 1.3.1 had updates to translations.

Just one year later, the Scratch website would be fully introduced, with Scratch 1.4, a growing community and drama...

Part 3: The Scratch website, Scratch 1.4 and 1.4.0.6

Scratch 1.4 was the latest and greatest update in the Scratch 1.x series. Launched officially in July 2nd, 2009 and had the most new features of any 1.x release.

It was big. It had a redrawn Scratch logo, LEGO WeDo motor controls with Motor Blocks, Asking and Answering in Sensing, new Operator and List blocks, and you had to click blocks once to run them! But what was really big was the new Scratch website.

This is the front page for Scratch 1.4. It had Featured Projects, introduced the Scratch Design Studio, What the Community is Remixing/Loving/Viewing pages, statistics, social media links (for Scratch Team), projects, galleries, search, user signin, login, and much much more! It was the biggest update yet to Scratch, and the website had it's first 1,000,000 users before 2010.

It introduced the now known Discussion Forums, the Scratch Wiki and the classic Scratch slogan: "imagine, program, share." Scratch 1.4 was the biggest update yet, but with that came community drama...

Part 4: The Community, Community Drama and Copyright

Since Scratch 1.4 also added remixing, some users started to complain about other users stealing their projects and not being banned, because it's "remixing" and it's "adding on to others' ideas". The remix controversy was way tinier compared to the removal of the Pac-Man project.

On July 29th, 2010, the Scratch team removed a project made by the user 124scratch. The project was similar to Pac-Man, a very popular arcade game, and Namco Bandai Games, the company that owned Pac-Man, requsted the removal of the project, since it may infringe their rights. But hundreds of Scratchers, and even Scratch Team members agreed that it did not broke copyright law, yet did not want to start a legal battle against the company.

On April 1st, 2011, Scratch hosted their April Fools' Day 2011 event, and a user by the name of "KajTheModerator" appeared. kaj, the original Scratcher, was a Scratcher who threatened to hack the Scratch team in an attempt for views and clout. KajTheModerator was an april fools prank and not a real user. He appeared again in April Fools' 2012, but has never came back since.

Part 5: The End of Scratch 1.x

That's all for this article. In the next article, we'll be talking about the even bigger update of Scratch 2.0, the supposed "golden age" of Scratch. Huge thanks for reading! If you liked this article make sure to like, comment and share. We'll be publishing more soon. :D

data.title: The Evolution of Scratch: Before Scratch Released (Part 1)
data.summary: This article series is about the evolution of Scratch 0.x, from a simple idea to a working programming language for kids.
data.content:
This is part 1 of an article series, "The Evolution of Scratch." See other parts:

Scratch website, community, and Scratch 1.0-1.4 (Part 2)

Scratch 2.0, Scratch's "Peak" and Scratch Community (Part 3)

Scratch 3.0, Modern Scratch Updates and the "downfall" of Scratch (Part 4)


The Evolution Of Scratch: Before Scratch Released

Part 1: Idea to Demo

In the early 2000s, the coding landscape was rough and not many people knew how to code. So in 2003, computer scientist Mitchel Restnick wanted to make a coding language that would teach kids coding, life skills and how to express themselves. The structure of Scratch was inspired by Logo, a programming language made in 1967 that used turtle graphics.

Restnick proposed the idea to the national Science Foundation and it was accepted. Shortly after, work began on Scratch and the first known version of Scratch was developed: Scratch 30Jun03.


Part 2: Older Versions (2003-2004)



The first versions of Scratch had the project runner on the left and the code/sprites on the right. Blocks were sharp and grabbed from the blocks categories (top-right) and dropped into the block storage (bottom-right). The first ever building blocks and logic gates were added, and to have multiple characters on the screen you had to manually add them in the sprite panel (top-right). There were no clones, no trigonometry, no message and error handling and no extensions.



Scratch continued to update and got its first ever meaningful update in 2004, where more block categories were added and the ability to draw sprites. The design changed, and now the block categories were on the left, the block storage in the middle and the project runner and sprites on the right. This is the first design that looks somewhat close to modern Scratch. It added X and Y position changing, directions and costumes.

But there was a problem. It missed crucial blocks, barely had text and font support and no way to upload costumes to it. But this all changed a year later...


Part 3: Scratch 0.x and 1.0 Betas (2004-2006)


This is Scratch 28May05, the most up to date 2005 version of Scratch! It introduced many quality-of-life features and a huge design change.

The editor is now slim with the majority of the space dedicated to the block storage, block categories were assigned their own colors (and most of these colors are used in Scratch today!) It introduced pen and effects for the first time, variables became rounded, the sqrt() block was added, and it made Scratch easy and fun to use.

The star button was used to add sprites, the UI was easier to read and use and the Stop button was redesigned to closer match what it is today. While it still wasn't close to Scratch 1.0, it was the biggest Scratch 0.x update of its time.



2006 was a massive year for Scratch. Above is a comparison of two of the largest versions of that time: 27Jul06 and 16Dec06.

27Jul06 added the if on edge, bounce, loudness, loud? blocks and microphone support. It was the version that changed the categories to the familiar "Motion, Looks, Sound, Pen, Control, Sensing, Numbers, Variables" used in Scratch 1.0.

But 16Dec06 was bigger. It added the old "forever if", next costume, next backdrop, "think" blocks, and stop all sounds blocks. It introduced the "Româna" language (hey that's my native language) and was the last update before Scratch 1.0.

2006 was also the year the Scratch website was released in beta. Users could download the most recent Scratch versions, but not share projects and comment yet. The Scratch website and Scratch 1.0 were released in 2007, and created the foundation for future Scratch versions...


Part 4: The End of Scratch 0.x

That's all for this article. In the next article, we'll be talking about the massive update of Scratch 1.0 and the Scratch website, features, community drama, forums, AND MORE!! Thanks for reading, and if you liked this article make sure to like it and comment. We'll be publishing more pretty soon. :)

data.title: 3D in Scratch Has Just Gotten Easier!
data.summary: Xelna_ has showcased an impressive pre-rendered movement system that brings realistic 3D environments into Scratch using Blender and frame-by-frame animation.
data.content:
xelna_ has released Pre-rendered Movement v1.4, a project demonstrating how realistic 3D movement can be achieved in Scratch using pre-rendered frames instead of real-time 3D rendering*

The project begins in Blender 3.4, where every possible movement is animated with keyframes. After rendering the animation into thousands of image frames, the frames are imported into TurboWarp to build the project before being brought into Scratch 3.0. (Link to project: https://scratch.mit.edu/projects/1362513266)

The idea was inspired by the horror game At Dead Of Night, which blends live-action footage with traditional gameplay. Rather than rendering a 3D world in real time, the game displays pre-rendered images to create the illusion of smooth 3D movement while keeping performance high.

According to @xelna_, this approach has several advantages. Because the environment is already rendered, computers only need to display image frames, allowing the project to run smoothly even though it appears graphically demanding. It also limits what players can see, making it more difficult to explore areas or access information outside of what the developer intends.

The creator says they plan to use this technique in a future Scratch project, with a murder mystery point-and-click game currently in mind.

Projects like this show how Scratch creators continue to push the platform beyond its intended limits, combining external tools such as Blender with Scratch to create experiences that look far more advanced than typical block-based projects.



*This article is created by Xelna himself, and looks a little bit AI-generated - take his advertising with a grain of salt. We do not want AI-generated content nor self-promotion on this platform; this article should not encourage others to self-advertise themselves here.

data.title: What we know about Scratch 4.0
data.summary: When 4.0? What 4.0? How 4.0? This article answers it all.
data.content:
If you're here, this means you're probably a Scratcher. And if you're a Scratcher, you've probably heard of the long awaited "Scratch 4.0". So many people hate the current state of Scratch, that their only hope is for Scratch 4.0 to come and change it for the better. This article answers everything you need to know about Scratch 4.0: updates in 4.0, updates related to 4.0 and other questions.


What is Scratch 4.0?

Scratch 4.0 (also known as "Scratch 4" and "4.0") will be the 4th major version of Scratch. Currently, we are in Scratch 3.0 (also known as "Scratch 3"). Acting as a major version of Scratch, Scratch 4.0 will bring the usual with major Scratch versions: a new UI, some new blocks and features etc. Major Scratch versions usually have some downtime for testing them, as Scratch 3.0 did in 2018/19: and Scratch 4.0 will do the same. Scratch 4.0 could possibly add AI features (the features in specific are unknown, but AI on Scratch could be possible), a new project tagging system and a refreshed Explore page.


When will Scratch 4.0 arrive?

Scratch 4.0 will come somewhere in 2027. Some Scratchers speculated Scratch 4.0 will come in 2025 (because past Scratch versions came every 6 years: 1.0 in 2007, 2.0 in 2013, and 3.0 in 2019). This is not true; the version times were purely coincidental and have nothing to do with when Scratch 4.0 will come.


Will 4.0 delete my projects?

When major Scratch versions arrive, you may expect some downtime on Scratch and you won't be able to access it. This does not mean that your projects, accounts, comments etc. will be "deleted"; the data you create on Scratch is stored in their backend (their servers), and the only thing that will temporarily shut down is the frontend (the website). Don't worry, your data is safe.


What is the NGP, and is the NGP Scratch 3.5/4.0?

The NGP ("new-generation platform") is the future version of the Scratch website, a Scratch website version that will act as the stepping stone between Scratch 3.0 and 4.0. It will bring a new and fixed Explore page, Google sign-on support and a domain change (from scratch.mit.edu to scratch.org). scratch.org domains already work in order to prepare for the NGP, and the NGP will take full effect at the end of 2026.

The NGP is not Scratch 3.5/4.0. The NGP is simply Scratch's way of making a good foundation for Scratch 4.0; it does not have anything more to do with the version.


So that's what we know about 4.0! Thanks for reading this article, and hope to see you later on ScratchNews!


This article talked in detail about Scratch 4.0. If you'd like to know more about past versions of Scratch, visit our part series "The Evolution Of Scratch":

Before Scratch Released (Part 1)

Scratch website, community, and Scratch 1.0-1.4 (Part 2)

Scratch 2.0, Scratch's "Peak" and Scratch Community (Part 3)

Scratch 3.0, Modern Scratch Updates and the "downfall" of Scratch (Part 4)

data.title: The Rise Of Katana Gaming
data.summary: From 5,000 to 25,000+ followers, in a single year
data.content:
If you Scratch, you've probably saw the Scratcher -Katana_Gaming-. He is one of the most popular Scratchers in the WORLD - over 6.6 million views, 100,000 loves and faves, and 15-30 followers a day on a consistent basis. If followers were money, he would've been on Forbes 30 under 30.

But how would someone build this unimaginable level of fame?

This article covers that, the history of him and what he uses to continue gathering followers.

Chapter 1 - From 0 to something

Katana joined in 2023. 2023 was the peak year of generic platformers - the explore page was full of them, and anywhere you looked thousands of Scratchers were entering the wave and mass-producing generic platformers. And he was no exception.

Eight of his first 12 projects are platformer-related, half of which are generic platformers. But this later turned out to be the biggest investment of his account, as he learned important fame-skills (thumbnail/description design, marketing) that would help him in the future.

But this is where the generic stops and the innovation starts to show.

He started experimenting with platformers and shifting ideas. His 6th ever project - Skylands - was already a major improvement from his old generic platformers, as the main premise changed from 'go right and win' to 'go left or right, here are some checkpoints along the way'. Skylands proved to be better than generic platformers: 800 more views than Resize, his #1 generic platformer. Then, he mixed generic platformers with the idea of 'Ninja', inspired from WillWam's popular Scratch game series Ninja: and made his best platformer yet.. Ninja. Over 200,000 views. He was in shock!

He continued creating generic platformers, trying more ideas along the way. Ninja 2 - over 150,000 views. Geometry Dash - 220,000 views. Football - over 230 THOUSAND views. This was his peak, his magnum opus... but then quit right before 2025 rolled around. In a few months, the game was about to change.


Chapter 2 - Researching the fame: and making it too

Katana revived his account in 2025, and went back to see nearly a million views in his account. It was 2025 - the first half was normal, the other trending froze and never recovered. While trending was still working, he began experimenting again with new ideas. This is when his thumbnails transitioned from image to animated GIF - and this was about to pay him big time. Combining the new Minecraft Movie, Skylands, and an animated GIF as a thumbnail, he created 'Only Up Minecraft' (now known as simply 'Minecraft'). He got half A MILLION views. This alerted him that Scratch never changed since the platformer era - and he used that to his advantage. He created Ninja 3. 750,000 views. And right before the Explore page broke, he made one last project before it... 'Geometry Wave'. Then Explore broke, and it stayed like that for months.

Let's play a guessing game. How many views do you think he got from that project? 100,000? 500,000? A million?

.....4. MILLION.

He got the entire state of Oklahoma to play his project. This was the final project that got him to 10,000 followers - and his most popular. Since trending broke, his next projects were only in the thousands of views... so he used another method to get himself more fame.


Chapter 3 - What he does now for followers, and what to learn from it

Katana uses a few methods to get followers in the present day. He uses studios to invite people, betting on the chance they'll like it and follow him. He created a network of people as his friends - helping him invite people to studios, in exchange for a valuable connection and experience in getting fame.

While these methods got him to 25,000, it's worth noting that he still can't get big followers without trending. No Scratcher can.


And in this next article, we're showing exactly why Trending is dead, how long it will be dead, and what you can do about it. Visit it here.

Bye, and thanks for reading.

data.title: What happened with Explore?
data.summary: No, the Explore page isn't gone. But something big about it is.
data.content:
Just about a year ago, the explore page was the biggest place to discover new Scratch projects, find good ones and make your projects popular. Today, the old explore is gone: there either are no projects, featured projects from years ago and inactive users suddenly being at the top of the page. What happened?


Well, something big happened. And still happening.

As you're reading through these lines, the Scratch Team is changing the way the Explore page and Search function, and by the end of this year Explore will be replaced. This is to make the foundation for a new Scratch - Scratch 4.0. The new Explore page is one of the features that Scratch teams wants to add to make Scratch a "NGP", next-generation platform.*


But why now, why freeze the Explore page in the process, and what is "NGP"?


1: The freeze


On July 2025, the indexer updated the Explore page with it's last project. What is the indexer?


The indexer is what Scratch uses to "update" projects. Before the freeze, when you shared a project, the indexer would save the statistics of the project: views, loves, faves and remixes. These are used to determine a project's position in Search and Explore. Occasionnally, the indexer would save the new statistics of the project: which is what causes it to move it's place in Scratch's Search and Explore. It is the machine that makes Scratch go round, maintaining the two biggest ways Scratchers find projects.


But on July 2025, this machine was put in pause. The Scratch Team found that people were using the Explore page and Search to show inappropriate projects, so they "temporarily" froze the indexer. For entire months, the Explore page stayed the same; some projects got banned in the process, some lived to obtain huge numbers. One of the last projects indexed was made by IncognitoOrange: and the project's view-count went from 20,000 to over 300,000.


2: The Explore page in 2026


On January 1st, 2026, all old Scratch projects in the Explore page were removed and replaced with recent projects from previously featured users: animations and games from October and November.


Throughout the winter, the Explore page slowly changed the projects to old featured projects. The Scratch Team still was working on the Explore page, so this "featured" page remained the default.


On March 2026, all the Explore page projects were removed. But never replaced. For a few days, the Explore page remained silent: not a single project was added. Then, some featured projects appeared: and now the Explore page was in it's yo-yo phase, switching from featured projects to no projects every few days.


Note that until March, Explore Studios was still fine: studios were still being indexed. Right around the no-project day, Scratch removed it, and replaced it with old featured studios. The only machine that updates its' gears now is Search Studios.


3: Where we are now


So the Explore page is still in it's yo-yo phase. And nothing has changed.


Except for the information that was given to us. On April 7th, 2026, Scratch Team published a new announcement for the "NGP": the Next-Generation Platform.*


The NGP is Scratch's way of making a meaningful update between Scratch 3.0 and Scratch 4.0. There will be new features added (such as customizable notifications and Google sign-on support), but more importantly, an upgraded Explore page. The NGP will have full effect by the end of the year, and there will be some downtimes throughout the summer to support it.

We can't really do anything to change the Explore page. All we can do is wait and hope for the best.



*This information was taken from the Scratch foundation at: https://scratchfoundation.org/announcements/ngp
